templates.pattern: An O(n²) algorithm processes a list of [N] items. Calculate the approximate number of operations performed.
templates.explanation:
O(n²) operations = n²
= [N]²
= [N] × [N]
= [RESULT]

O(n²) algorithms become very slow for large inputs. Doubling n quadruples the operations. Bubble sort, selection sort and insertion sort all have O(n²) worst-case complexity.

templates.pattern: An O(n log n) algorithm processes a list of [N] items where N is a power of 2. Calculate the approximate number of operations.
templates.explanation:
O(n log n) operations = n × log₂(n)
= [N] × log₂([N])
= [N] × [log2(N)]
= [RESULT]

O(n log n) is much more efficient than O(n²) for large n. Merge sort, quicksort (average) and heapsort all achieve O(n log n). For n=1024 this is 10,240 vs 1,048,576 for O(n²).

templates.pattern: An algorithm performs [TOTAL] operations across [N] insertions using amortised analysis. Calculate the amortised cost per operation.
templates.explanation:
Amortised cost = total operations ÷ number of insertions
= [TOTAL] ÷ [N]
= [RESULT] per operation

Amortised analysis spreads the cost of expensive operations over many cheap ones. Dynamic arrays use amortised O(1) insertion — most inserts are O(1) but occasional resizing is O(n).

templates.pattern: A complete graph has [V] vertices. Calculate the total number of edges in the graph.
templates.explanation:
Edges in complete graph = V(V−1) ÷ 2
= [V] × ([V]−1) ÷ 2
= [V] × [V-1] ÷ 2
= [RESULT]

In a complete graph every vertex connects to every other vertex. Each of the V vertices has V−1 connections but each edge is counted twice so we divide by 2.

templates.pattern: A spanning tree is created from a connected graph with [V] vertices. Calculate the number of edges in the spanning tree.
templates.explanation:
Spanning tree edges = V − 1
= [V] − 1
= [RESULT]

A spanning tree connects all vertices with the minimum number of edges and no cycles. It always has exactly V−1 edges. A minimum spanning tree minimises the total edge weight.

templates.pattern: A minimum spanning tree connects [V] vertices using edges of weights [W1], [W2] and [W3] (the three smallest edges that form no cycle). Calculate the total weight of the MST.
templates.explanation:
MST total weight = sum of selected edge weights
= [W1] + [W2] + [W3]
= [RESULT]

Kruskal's and Prim's algorithms both find the minimum spanning tree. Kruskal's sorts edges by weight and adds them if they don't form a cycle. Prim's grows from a starting vertex.

templates.pattern: A quicksort algorithm processes a list of [N] items where N is a power of 2. Calculate the average number of comparisons using n × log₂(n).
templates.explanation:
Quicksort average comparisons = n × log₂(n)
= [N] × log₂([N])
= [N] × [log2(N)]
= [RESULT]

Quicksort averages O(n log n) but degrades to O(n²) for already-sorted lists with poor pivot selection. Randomised pivot selection avoids this worst case in practice.

templates.pattern: A perfect binary tree has a height of [H] levels (root is level 0). Calculate the total number of nodes in the tree.
templates.explanation:
Total nodes in perfect binary tree = 2^(h+1) − 1
= 2^([H]+1) − 1
= 2^[H+1] − 1
= [2^(H+1)] − 1
= [RESULT]

A perfect binary tree has all leaf nodes at the same level. The number of nodes doubles at each level. Height 10 gives 2¹¹ − 1 = 2047 nodes.

templates.pattern: A recursive algorithm divides a problem of size [N] in half at each call. Calculate the maximum call stack depth where N is a power of 2.
templates.explanation:
Stack depth = log₂(n)
= log₂([N])
= [RESULT]

Each recursive call halves the problem size. The recursion stops when size reaches 1. This log₂(n) stack depth is why divide-and-conquer algorithms use O(log n) space.

templates.pattern: An algorithm takes [T1] seconds on 1 processor. The same algorithm takes [TP] seconds on [P] processors. Calculate the parallel speedup.
templates.explanation:
Parallel speedup = T₁ ÷ Tₚ
= [T1] ÷ [TP]
= [RESULT]

Perfect speedup with p processors would give speedup = p. In practice Amdahl's Law limits speedup because some parts of the algorithm cannot be parallelised.
